t: When her grandfather died, Ayesha was left a steel trunk, a walking stick, and a rule she never understood.
"Paper is a promise. Gold is a weight."
At the bottom of the trunk, wrapped in red velvet, was a small bar of gold.
One tola. Eleven point six six grams.
And folded beneath it, a receipt from a jeweller's shop in Anarkali.
The year: 1950. The price: forty-three rupees.
This morning, the same tola is worth Rs 435,720.
About ten thousand times more.
The gold has not changed. Not by a single grain.
So what did?
Her father had done everything right. For thirty years he worked, and kept every rupee he saved in the bank.
But a hundred rupees saved in the year 2000 buys about thirteen rupees of goods today.
One man trusted a promise. The other trusted a weight.
This film follows Ayesha's question across five thousand years.
It begins with something that measures every life on earth,
and quietly shrinks.
Escape the Matrix.
Every number you will hear has a source you can open. One hundred and one of them.
Every forecast has a date, a probability, and a test that could prove it wrong.
Because experts are often wrong. In December 2021, the Federal Reserve expected rates near 1% a year later. They ended above 4%.
So we will not sell you a prediction. We will show you worlds, and keep score.
Part One. The Shrinking Ruler.
Imagine measuring a room with a ruler that loses a millimetre every year.
The room never moves. But every year, it seems a little bigger.
That is exactly how money measures your life.
In 1928, the economist Irving Fisher gave it a name: the money illusion.
If your salary rises 10% while prices rise 12%, you feel richer,
and you are poorer.
Not a secret society. Not a conspiracy. A unit of measurement that shrinks, in plain sight.
In America, $100 from 1913 buys $2.95 of goods today.
The rest was not stolen in a night. It was measured away, one year at a time.
In Pakistan, the ruler shrinks faster.
The rupee was born in 1948 at 3.31 to the dollar.
4.76 in 1955. About 11 in 1972. It passed 100 in 2013, and 200 in 2022.
In the crisis of 2023, it touched 300. Today, it is 277.
Against the dollar, Rs 100 from 1950 is now worth Rs 1.2.
Now look at the same years through Daada's tola.
Rs 43 in 1950. Rs 435,720 today.
Over every ten-year span since 1980, the rupee price of gold has risen.
Not once has it fallen.
But this is not a film that sells gold.
Measured against ordinary prices, gold today is near its most expensive level ever: 12.5, against a long-run average of 3.3.
From heights like this, gold's next decade has usually been poor.
A ruler that never shrinks can still be bought at the wrong price.
So Ayesha asked a different question. Not, what is it worth? But: who must keep a promise for it to be worth anything?
The economist John Exter drew money as an upside-down pyramid.
At the narrow base: gold, which is nobody's promise.
Above it: cash, deposits, bonds, $365 trillion of debt, and at the very top, derivatives.
The higher you stand, the more people must keep their word for you to be paid.
A gold coin in your hand needs no one. A gold ETF needs a fund, a custodian and an exchange. A gold CFD needs only your broker.
When European regulators forced brokers to publish, 74 to 89% of retail accounts were losing money.
But who decided that the ruler should shrink? And when?
To find out, Ayesha had to go back five thousand years.
Part Two. The Weight.
Mesopotamia. Five thousand years ago.
The textbooks say people bartered first: a goat for a sack of grain. The evidence says otherwise.
Temple scribes kept accounts in silver shekels two thousand years before the first coin was struck.
The anthropologist Caroline Humphrey searched for a true barter economy. She found none. Anywhere. Ever.
Barter comes after money fails: cigarettes in prison camps, Germany in 1923, Russia in the nineties.
The monies that lasted shared one secret: nobody tampered with their weight.
The Byzantine solidus held for seven centuries.
The Islamic dinar was struck at 4.25 grams of gold.
Sher Shah Suri's silver rupiya gave the rupee its name.
And in 1833, the British fixed the tola at 180 grains: the weight of the silver rupee.
Daada's bar is measured in the weight of a coin that no longer exists. The money changed. The ruler stayed.
But kings always found a quieter way to pay their bills.
Rome's denarius fell to less than 5% silver.
Henry the Eighth cut England's coins from 92.5% silver to 25%, until the copper showed through on the king's nose. They called him Old Coppernose.
Long before, the prophet Isaiah had named it: thy silver is become dross.
Today nobody clips coins. Inflation above the interest paid to savers does the same work, silently. It is called financial repression.
Paper money began as a receipt for something real.
Every paper money that collapsed had printed more receipts than it had things.
And every gold standard ended in war or depression: 1797. 1914. 1933. 1971.
Under metal, American prices in 1913 were 42% lower than in 1800. Since 1913, they have multiplied 34 times.
On the fifteenth of August, 1971, the last anchor was cut.
The dollar was no longer a receipt for gold.
It was simply a dollar.
Since that night, gold has risen from $41 to $4,195, and the dollar has lost 88% of its buying power.
But not its throne.
With no anchor left, money would no longer be dug from the ground.
It would be made by a machine.
Part Three. The Machine.
Most people believe banks lend out the money that savers deposit.
The Bank of England says the opposite: whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit.
97% of the money the British public holds is bank deposits, not notes and coins.
In America, the money supply stands at a record $23.34 trillion.
In the 1730s, a banker named Richard Cantillon noticed something about new money.
It does not arrive everywhere at once. Those nearest the tap spend it first, before prices rise.
Those at the end of the pipe receive it last, after prices have already risen.
Today, America's labour share has fallen to 52.8%, the lowest on record, while the top 1% hold a third of household wealth.
The machine now runs on debt.
$40.1 trillion for America. $365 trillion for the world. Interest above $1 trillion a year.
A country that owes this much in its own currency has three exits: grow, inflate, or restructure.
The easiest is the oldest: let the ruler shrink.
And no, America cannot erase its debt by revaluing its gold. Its gold covers 2.7% of the debt. To cover all of it, gold would need to be priced at $153,335 an ounce.
The machine has a shape, and it is published.
29 systemic banks. Three index giants with more than $31 trillion. Three rating agencies with 94% of all ratings. Two card networks.
And one sanctions office that can cut any bank off the dollar.
It is not a cartel meeting in secret. It sits in annual reports.
In 2022, the machine showed its power. About $300 billion of Russia's reserves were frozen.
Every central bank on earth learned that its dollars are someone else's promise.
Their answer was Daada's answer: gold. More than 1,000 tonnes a year, from 2022 to 2024.
The dollar's share of world reserves has slipped from 71.5% to 56.7%.
Now the next pipes are being laid.
Dollar stablecoins: $316 billion. A digital euro, planned for 2029.
A stablecoin is a dollar with a faster engine, and an issuer who can freeze it.
A central bank digital currency is a liability with a camera.
For Pakistan, the danger is not that the machine collapses. It is that it runs dry.
In 2008 and in 2020, the world scrambled for dollars, and the rupee fell.
For a country with debts owed in dollars, the shortage is the crisis.
Daada never read an economics book.
But he had read something much older.
Part Four. The Scriptures.
Ask six traditions what day it is, and you get six answers.
2026 in the Gregorian calendar. 1448 after the Hijra. 5787 in the Hebrew calendar.
More than 5,100 years into the Kali Yuga. 2569 in the Buddhist era. 558 in the Sikh calendar.
Ask them when the end will come, and all six give the same answer.
No one knows the hour.
The Quran forbids riba, and permits trade.
It condemns hoarding gold and silver without zakat, and warns those who give short measure in the scales.
And in the story of Yusuf, it records the oldest reserve plan we know:
seven good years: store the harvest in its ear. Seven hard years will consume what you stored.
The hadith speak of signs: barefoot herders competing in tall buildings; a time when people will not care whether what they take is lawful.
But the report most often shared to sell gold, that one day only the dinar and the dirham will benefit people, has a chain graded weak.
A weak report cannot carry the weight that marketing puts on it.
For a Muslim household in Pakistan, the rules are practical: zakat on gold above 7.5 tola, and a constitutional deadline to remove riba from the economy by the first of January, 2028.
The Bible's last-days passages are strikingly about money.
A measure of wheat for a penny: a whole day's wage for a day's bread.
The borrower is servant to the lender.
The Torah wrote the first debt release into law: every seventh year, the Shmita. Every fiftieth, the Jubilee.
Proclaim liberty throughout all the land: the words cast on America's Liberty Bell.
And the Talmud's oldest portfolio: a third in land, a third in business, a third at hand.
The Puranas describe the Kali Yuga as an age when the minds of men are wholly occupied in acquiring wealth.
Yet prosperity is one of life's four aims, and gold is Lakshmi's metal.
The Buddha's advice to a householder is a budget 2,500 years old: one part to enjoy, two parts to invest in work, the fourth kept against misfortune.
And the Sikh Gurus give three pillars: earn by honest work, share what you have, and remember God.
Read together, six traditions across three thousand years agree.
The late age loves money. Interest is restricted. Weights must be honest.
Store in the years of plenty. Share. And no one knows the hour.
"Save in the good years. The hard years come on their own."
This decade, two events will be called signs.
On the second of August 2027, a total eclipse will cross Makkah. In April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will pass closer than our satellites.
When an eclipse fell on the day his infant son died, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: the sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or the life of anyone.
Notice the event. Ignore the omen. Keep the plan.
We even tested the Shmita years. In 22 of them since 1874, American shares averaged minus 2.3% after inflation, against plus 10.3% in all other years.
A gap that large appears by chance about once in a thousand shuffles.
But nothing links markets to a calendar. An echo without a cause is a test to register, not a bet.
So if no one knows the hour,
how do you prepare for a future you cannot see?
Part Five. Six Worlds.
In 2005, Philip Tetlock tested 82,361 expert forecasts. Long-range calls barely beat chance.
So instead of one prediction, the atlas draws a map of worlds, with odds that add to a hundred.
History helps. No reserve currency has ever ended on a single day.
Portugal, Spain, the Dutch, France, Britain: each fell in steps. Sterling fell over sixty years: 1931, 1949, 1967, 1976.
There are five ways the dollar's story could go.
Slow erosion: 25%. Managed devaluation: 31%. Debasement: 16%.
The dramatic collapse everyone sells, a disorderly break: just 4%.
And in nearly a quarter of futures, the dollar wins.
Anyone who sells you a dated collapse is selling the least likely path as a certainty.
Ten forces will decide the decade. Debt, central-bank buying and war lean toward hard assets. Artificial intelligence and stretched valuations lean against them.
They resolve into six worlds for 2036.
AI Dividend, 16%: productivity booms, the dollar firms, and gold falls back to $3,400.
Quiet Repression, 31%, the likeliest: capped yields, 3 to 4% inflation, a softer dollar. Gold to $9,000.
Long Grind, 19%: nothing breaks, and everything muddles.
Debasement, 18%: politics overrides the Fed, inflation runs at 6 to 7%, and gold reaches $16,000.
Debt Deflation, 8%: a credit bust, and a Japan-style chill.
And Fracture, 8%: war in the Gulf or over Taiwan, sanctions, and rationed trade.
Weighted together, at the end of 2036:
Gold $8,740. Silver $148. Brent $96. Bitcoin $347,000. The S&P 500, 11,565.
And 480 rupees to the dollar.
But in today's money, gold is $5,680, and oil just $63.
For Ayesha's family, the numbers come home.
Every $10 on oil adds about Rs 19 a litre. The weighted path takes petrol from Rs 397 to Rs 605 by 2036.
And Daada's tola, Rs 4.36 lakh today, reaches Rs 16.2 lakh on the weighted path.
Bitcoin runs on a clock. Each halving cycle's gain has been smaller: 112 times, then 21, then 7.9.
By 2036, 99.2% of all bitcoin will exist. And its range is the widest in the atlas: from $63,000 to $774,000.
Where the model is kinder than history, it says so.
The council's scored calls so far carry a Brier score of 0.22. 12% better than a coin flip. A start, not proof.
But the six worlds reveal one hard truth.
Every single asset has a world where it loses.
Part Six. The Escape.
We ran every asset through all six worlds.
Gold's worst world is AI Dividend. Shares' worst is Fracture. Cash loses in Debasement.
Every asset has a losing world.
The balanced mixes have none.
For a Pakistani saver, the result is uncomfortable.
Rupee deposits, after tax, lost real value in all six worlds.
Gold by the tola gained in five. The KSE-100 led in four.
And a simple balanced mix of deposits, gold, shares and some dollars gained in every one.
We back-tested the oldest advice too, on 53 years of market data.
The Buddha's split, two parts business and the rest kept against misfortune, earned 6% a year after inflation,
and beat the classic 60-40 portfolio, with a smaller fall.
So here is the playbook.
Keep two sets of books: one in rupees, one in grams, litres and hours.
Own assets, not only promises. Avoid costly debt and leverage.
Keep a granary. Diversify across worlds, not just assets. Size for survival.
And ignore anyone who sells a date.
Before you believe any collapse video, including this one, ask six questions.
Where is each number from? Is there a date? What is the base rate?
What would prove it wrong? Who profits if you believe it? Has the speaker ever been scored?
Twenty gauges will tell us which world is arriving: the ten-year yield, real rates, the dollar, central-bank gold, Brent, the rupee, Pakistan's reserves.
And twenty dated calls go into the ledger, to be scored in public.
Gold at or above $5,000 at the end of 2027: 20%. A US recession beginning by the end of 2028: 50%. Gold higher than today at the end of 2036: 83%.
An atlas that is never scored is a sermon, not research.
The rain had stopped.
Ayesha wrapped the tola back in its velvet. She did not sell it. She did not rush to buy more, either.
She opened a notebook and drew two columns. On the left, rupees. On the right: grams, litres, and hours.
Her grandfather had not escaped the matrix. No one can.
But he had seen through it.
Every scripture, checked against the data, points to the same escape.
Earn honestly. Avoid usurious debt. Never cheat on weight.
Store part of every good year in something that keeps. Give part away.
And ignore anyone who claims to know the hour.
Paper is a promise. Gold is a weight. And the hour belongs to no one.
Escape the Matrix.
A film by The Gold Council.
